name: The World of AI: Power and Cooling section on datacenter energy
title: The World of AI: Power and Cooling section on datacenter energy
answer: Power and Cooling is a section page from The World of AI, an AI reference site. It lists three curated entries on how AI datacenters get electricity and cooling, covering grid connection, generation contracts and liquid cooling. Its most useful point is the cited Department of Energy 2024 LBNL analysis: datacenters used about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and are projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028, with AI as the driver.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this page, titled Power and Cooling, as part of its AI ecosystem technology and core infrastructure section. It is a section index, not a report, and it says it holds three power and cooling entries, each curated with a verified vendor or primary source and re-verified daily. Its stated scope is how an AI datacenter gets electricity and gets rid of heat, including grid connection and interconnection queues, generation contracted to serve the load, and the shift from air to liquid cooling. It says individual facilities are covered in Data Centers and racks and interconnect in other hardware sections. The page gives a retrieval date of 2026-09-29 and says pages are rebuilt daily from primary sources.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page is a section index for Power and Cooling. It says the section has three entries, each curated with a verified vendor or primary source and re-verified daily. The section covers how an AI datacenter gets electricity and gets rid of heat: grid connection and interconnection queues, the generation contracted to serve the load, and the shift from air to liquid cooling that dense GPU racks forced. It directs readers elsewhere for individual facilities, which are in Data Centers, and for racks and interconnect, which are in other hardware sections. The main substantive claim is attributed to DOE's 2024 LBNL report: datacenters consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and are projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028, with AI as the driver. The page says this trajectory reflects a hard constraint on AI scaling, because the grid cannot expand as fast as compute demand grows. Even modest adoption of AI training and inference at scale will require either new generation capacity, storage, or load shifting, none of which are built yet. The 6.7 to 12% range signals uncertainty about how fast AI deployment actually happens, depending on factors the electricity numbers alone cannot capture. The page also describes the wider site as an AI atlas rebuilt daily from primary sources, with search across state AI laws, a lawsuit tracker, glossary, tools directory, AI companies, research library, MCP server registry, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators and weekly digests.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that the Power and Cooling section has three entries. It attributes to DOE's 2024 LBNL report the figures that datacenters consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and are projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028, with AI as the driver. It states that the grid cannot expand as fast as compute demand grows, that even modest adoption of AI training and inference at scale will require new generation capacity, storage, or load shifting, and that none of these are built yet. It says the 6.7 to 12% range signals uncertainty about how fast AI deployment happens. It also says entries are curated with a verified vendor or primary source and re-verified daily.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in Energy can use this page as a short, cited pointer to the power constraint on AI scaling. It names the DOE 2024 LBNL report as the basis for the 4.4% and 6.7 to 12% figures, so it is useful for tracking datacenter electricity demand and the grid, generation, storage and load shifting issues that follow. It also maps the section's scope to interconnection queues, contracted generation and the move from air to liquid cooling, which are practical energy concerns for dense GPU deployments. Because the page is a curated index rather than a full analysis, it works best as a starting point and as a daily re-verified tracker of a small number of entries.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Energy

sections.body: This is a section landing page with only three entries, so it does not provide the full content of those entries or the underlying DOE report. It gives no methodology, regional breakdown, or detailed data behind the 4.4% and 6.7 to 12% figures. It does not cover individual datacenter facilities or racks and interconnect, which it says are in other sections. The page is partly commercial, carrying promotions for books by Stephen R. Jordan, an SRJ Consulting novel, and a list of audit products. It gives a retrieval date of 2026-09-29 but no publication date for the DOE analysis beyond 2024, and it notes that the projection range reflects uncertainty.
